title: Over 200,000 H-1B Applicants Paid $100,000 Each This Year. Most of Them Are Likely Indian.
excerpt: DHS Secretary Mullin told the Senate that 70 percent of this year's H-1B applicants opted for expedited processing at the cost introduced by Trump's 2025 proclamation.
body:
The number is staggering even by the standards of American immigration's pay-to-play era: more than 200,000 H-1B visa applicants paid $100,000 each to fast-track their petitions in fiscal year 2026. That is roughly $20 billion in fees for a single visa category in a single year.

Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin disclosed the figure on Tuesday while testifying before the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee. Of the 286,000 H-1B applications received this fiscal year, more than 70 percent opted for expedited processing — paying a fee that did not even exist two years ago.

"We had 286,000 applicants a year to date for the H-1B visas. Out of those, over 200,000 of them paid $100,000 to be able to come in because it allows us to process them in a little bit faster of a manner," Mullin told the subcommittee, responding to Senator Susan Collins's question about doctor shortages in rural America.

What the Fee Buys

The answer, in practical terms, is time. Applicants who pay the $100,000 have their cases processed in approximately 15 days. Everyone else waits roughly 7.5 months. For a software engineer whose project timeline is measured in sprints, or a hospital that needs a specialist before flu season, that gap is the difference between a career and a missed opportunity.

The $100,000 fee was introduced through a presidential proclamation signed by Donald Trump in September 2025. It applies to employers filing new H-1B petitions for individuals currently outside the United States. The fee was immediately challenged in federal courts — the U.S. Chamber of Commerce filed suit in the District of Columbia, arguing it violates the Immigration and Nationality Act's requirement that fees reflect actual processing costs. A separate coalition of immigration advocacy organisations brought a parallel challenge in Northern California. Neither case has been resolved.

The Diaspora Dimension

For the Indian tech community in the United States, the numbers carry a specific gravity. Indian nationals have historically received between 70 and 75 percent of all H-1B visas granted each year. If that proportion holds, more than 140,000 of the applicants who paid the $100,000 fee are likely Indian — representing roughly ₹1.33 lakh crore ($14 billion) in fees from a single diaspora community.

The fee has reshaped the economics of hiring foreign talent. Major IT services firms — TCS, Infosys, Wipro, and HCL — have been steadily localising their U.S. workforces over the past two years, with 50 to 80 percent of their American employees now hired domestically. The $100,000 fee accelerates that shift. Smaller companies and startups, which cannot absorb the cost as easily, face a harder calculus.

A Two-Track System

Mullin himself acknowledged during the hearing that the system may need adjustment. He signalled flexibility on the fee in certain cases, suggesting the department could provide relief for sectors facing acute shortages — particularly healthcare and education in rural areas. Senator Collins had pressed him specifically on the difficulty of recruiting doctors for underserved communities when the visa process itself costs six figures.

The DHS secretary also indicated support for making it easier for seasonal H-2B workers to return to the United States, a program that supplies temporary labour to hospitality, construction, and seafood processing industries.

What It Means for Indians Abroad

The H-1B program has long been the primary legal pathway for Indian professionals entering the American workforce. The $100,000 fee does not close that pathway, but it fundamentally changes who can afford to walk it. Companies with deep pockets will continue to sponsor talent. Early-career professionals, international students transitioning from F-1 visas, and workers at smaller firms face a barrier that did not exist before September 2025.

H-1B registrations for fiscal year 2026 had already dropped to 358,000, down from 478,000 the prior year — a 25 percent decline that predated the full impact of the fee. The combination of rising costs, legal uncertainty, and an increasingly hostile political climate around immigration has begun to alter the calculation for an entire generation of Indian engineers and scientists weighing their futures.

The legal challenges to the fee remain pending. Until the courts rule, the $100,000 is the price of admission — and 200,000 people have already paid it.
